categories.name: Unless / Without / Except
categories.description: Single negation indicators, negate the sufficient

questions.sentence: You will fail unless you study.
questions.correct: If you don't fail, then you studied.
questions.wrong: If you study, then you will not fail.
questions.explanation: "Unless" is a negate-the-sufficient word. Negate the first part: "you will fail" becomes "you don't fail." That's your sufficient. The second part, "you study," stays the same and goes in the necessary. Not fail → Study. The other answer is incorrect. "You study" is the second part of the sentence, so it goes in the necessary. The other answer puts it in the sufficient.

questions.explanation: "Without" is a negate-the-sufficient word. Negate the first part: "sunlight" becomes "no sunlight." That's your sufficient. The second part, "plants wilt," stays the same and goes in the necessary. /Sunlight → Wilt. The other answer is incorrect. It negates the second part. With without, you negate only the first part and keep the second part the same.

categories.name: No / None / Cannot
categories.description: Single negation indicators, negate the necessary

questions.sentence: No doctor would recommend this treatment.
questions.correct: If someone is a doctor, then they would not recommend this treatment.
questions.wrong: Some doctors would recommend this treatment.
questions.explanation: "No" is a negate-the-necessary word. Keep the first part the same: "doctor" is your sufficient. Then negate the second part: "would recommend this treatment" becomes "would not recommend this treatment." Doctor → /Recommend treatment. The other answer says the opposite.

categories.name: Combined: Cannot + Unless / Without
categories.description: Two negation indicators together acting as conditional triggers, negations cancel each other out.

questions.sentence: You cannot vote unless you are registered.
questions.correct: If you voted, then you are registered.
questions.wrong: If you are registered, then you voted.
questions.explanation: "Cannot" is a negate-the-necessary word and "unless" is a negate-the-sufficient word. Two negatives cancel, so read the sentence without them: if you vote, you are registered. Vote → Registered. The other answer is incorrect. "You are registered" is the second part of the sentence, so it goes in the necessary. The other answer puts it in the sufficient.
